rv.q: Sharp delivers these speeches like a stream of burning rocks tumbling into our laps.
When Sharp is centre stage, it’s something staggering.
At the centre, Sharp is tremendous.
I'd sit through this long, uninterrupted 110-minute show all over again, just for Odysseus's brilliant pizza gag.
Patchy, then – but when Paradise lands a punch, you feel it in your guts.
It effectively undermines the notion of heroic masculinity, but also holds the actors back from humanising their parts.
It’s all so rich, so powerful, so triumphantly theatrical and savagely beautiful that it’s overwhelming.
In Ian Rickson’s production this blending of ancient and modern seems seamless and performances fizzing with energy grip the attention for nearly two hours without interval.
This show is slick and polished, and, most importantly, it has teeth.
Kae Tempest is aiming their bow at too many targets and unfortunately, unlike Philoctetes, a lot of Tempest’s arrows miss the bull’s eye completely.
This doesn’t feel like a work of art but a symptom of mental illness.
Best of all is the decision not to update Philoctetes’ weapon to a gun or missile-launcher.

cn.t: Tempest's bold, all-female adaptation of Sophocles divides critics. Most praise Lesley Sharp's extraordinary central performance and the contemporary relevance, though some find the sprawling production uneven and its radical reimagining doesn't fully cohere.
